/SATURDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
Issued at 211 AM CDT Thu Oct 29 2026

Saturday, a longwave trough will remain across the western United 
States, gradually progressing eastward through the day. Ahead of 
this trough, upper-level ridging will continue to amplify across the 
northern Plains, resulting in height rises across the region. 
Moisture advection will persist throughout the day, with PWAT values 
ranging from 150 to 250 percent of normal for this time of year. A 
weak southern-stream disturbance is expected to track just south of 
the forecast area, though precipitation chances should remain low as 
the better forcing for ascent remains displaced to the south. Given 
the increased moisture within the lower to middle levels, along with 
some weak synoptic-scale ascent, considerable cloud cover is 
expected across the area Saturday. Highs should remain in the lower 
60s across southern and eastern Nebraska, where the greatest cloud 
cover is expected, with middle 60s farther northwest where more 
clearing is possible. Overnight lows Saturday night should remain in 
the middle to upper 40s, as persistent low-level moisture and cloud 
cover limit radiational cooling.

Sunday, the western longwave trough is expected to evolve into a 
closed upper-level low across the Desert Southwest, resulting in 
strengthening southwesterly flow aloft across the central Plains. 
Much of Sunday should remain dry, though increasing southeasterly 
surface winds will support continued moisture advection, with 
dewpoints potentially reaching the middle 50s by Sunday afternoon. 
Considerable cloud cover is expected to persist, especially as 
moisture continues to increase ahead of the approaching system. This 
should limit daytime warming, with highs generally in the lower 60s 
across the area. By Sunday evening into the overnight hours, model 
guidance indicates a strengthening low-level jet, increasing upper-
level divergence, and enhanced warm air advection and 
frontogenetical forcing within the lower to middle levels. These 
features, combined with increasing moisture transport ahead of a 
developing lee-side surface low across the central High Plains, 
should provide sufficient forcing for more widespread showers and 
thunderstorms across the forecast area. Given the anomalously moist 
air mass and potentially strong synoptic-scale ascent, locally heavy 
rainfall may be possible, particularly where stronger forcing 
becomes established.Instability currently appears limited, partially 
due to relatively warm temperatures aloft and weak mid-level lapse 
rates, which should keep the overall severe weather threat low. 
However, with strong vertical wind shear expected, a few stronger 
thunderstorms cannot be ruled out, especially if sufficient 
instability develops ahead of the surface low. Confidence is 
increasing in more widespread precipitation Sunday night into Monday 
morning, though uncertainty remains regarding the placement of the 
heaviest rainfall.

Monday into the middle of next week, considerable uncertainty 
remains regarding the evolution and eventual track of the upper-
level system. The GFS/GEFS suite continues to favor a stronger and 
more northerly solution, while the ECMWF/EPS suite generally 
supports a farther south track, which could limit precipitation 
potential across portions of the forecast area beyond Monday 
morning. Recent global model trends have also begun to suggest a 
more pronounced split-flow pattern, with limited interaction between 
the northern- and southern-stream disturbances. If this solution 
materializes, the strongest upper-level forcing could remain 
displaced north and south of the region, limiting the potential for 
more widespread precipitation behind the surface low. In contrast, 
previous model runs had suggested greater interaction between the 
northern and southern streams, potentially resulting in a deeper and 
more amplified storm system. Such a scenario could support stronger 
forcing for ascent across the central Plains, including the 
potential for a more organized deformation zone on the northwest 
side of the system. This would favor a longer duration of 
precipitation across portions of western and north-central Nebraska. 
The strength and placement of the upper-level ridge across southern 
Canada will also play an important role in the eventual track of the 
system, as a stronger ridge could favor a farther south storm track 
and potentially shift the greatest precipitation chances away from 
the forecast area. Given these competing scenarios, confidence 
remains low regarding precipitation coverage and duration Monday 
into early next week. While confidence is increasing in widespread 
precipitation Sunday night into Monday morning, the potential for 
additional precipitation beyond that period remains considerably 
more uncertain. Trends will continue to be monitored as model 
guidance begins to converge on a more consistent solution. In
